newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RUGBY UNION-FIJI VICTORY PROVES HEADACHE FOR COACH.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-FIJI VICTORY PROVES HEADACHE FOR COACH.

text.p: Fiji will grind to a halt on Friday when the tiny Pacific nation enjoys a public holiday to honour its world-beating seven-a-side rugby union team.
But amid the euphoria over Fiji's triumph in last month's prestigious Hong Kong Sevens tournament, the man charged with ensuring Fiji's overall rugby success has mixed feelings.

While acknowledging the scale of Fiji's achievement in beating the major rugby powers in the seven-a-side version of the game, national test coach Brad Johnstone believes the victory may prove bitter-sweet.
"One thing's for sure, it will definitely make my job harder," the 46-year-old former New Zealand test forward told Reuters in a telephone interview from Fiji.
According to Johnstone, who played 13 tests at prop between 1976 and 1980, Fiji's prowess at the abridged form of the game works against them at the 15-a-side level, his own area of responsibility.
And he says the true measure of performance in rugby union can only be judged by results in the full-scale game.

Yet in Fiji, it is sevens rugby, regarded as an enjoyable distraction elsewhere in the world, that dominates thinking. When schoolkids across Fiji's 300 islands get the day off on Friday, it will be sevens, not 15-a-side, that they will play.

The Fijians delighted crowds in Hong Kong with their vibrant attacking game, leaving one beaten opponent, Welshman Darren Edwards, to declare them "in a class of their own" after their record seventh win in the tournament.
But at test level, those attacking skills have proved inadequate to compensate for other weaknesses. Fiji are currently no match for the established nations such as Australia, New Zealand or England.
And unless they switch their attention away from sevens, the gap will only widen, Johnstone believes.
"Being a former All Black I find it all totally frustrating," he said. "There is a lack of perception of what is real rugby."

Johnstone believes Fiji have the potential, if properly directed, to transfer their prowess at sevens to a far bigger, and more significant stage -- the 15-a-side World Cup, which will next be staged in Wales in 1999.
"Fijian players have tremendous leg strength, they're naturally fit and agile, and their basic handling and passing skills are outstanding. They are a joy to work with," he said.
Fiji's current standing at 15-a-side will be tested next month when they travel to New Zealand for a six-match tour, culminating in a one-off test against the All Blacks on June 14.
Despite the significance of the fixture, Johnstone sees his side suffering because of Fiji's obsession with sevens.
The tour to New Zealand clashes with two sevens tournaments overseas, Johnstone says, and he expects to lose out when it comes to selection priorities.
"I am going to find it very hard to get all the players I want. If everything goes in my favour, I expect the team to face New Zealand will be about two-thirds full strength."
In Johnstone's view, the explanation for the concentration on sevens is simple: money. Or the lack of it.

Sevens is easy to organise, easy to play, and does not require the specialist training methods or equipment needed for the more complex 15-a-side game and on a poor island like Fiji, that's paramount.
"During the last 10 years, players elsewhere have lived in the gym, working on fitness and strength programmes. Fijians just run -- they have no training facilities."
"The players are woefully weak in their upper bodies. Some of them could do no more than two chin ups in a fitness test. That's what you'd expect at an average club side overseas."
In sevens, where brute force is secondary to speed, upper-body strength is not the telling factor.

But in the full game it is vital. Johnstone says Fiji cannot yet compete against the top sides at 15-a-side, denying rugby supporters the opportunity to see some of the most naturally gifted players in the world performing to their potential.
"If my players could train every day in the professional environment other nations take for granted they would develop out of this world. They have an amazing ability to play rugby.
"I truly believe they are capable of winning the World Cup. It might take a decade but I believe it is possible."
